slides.title: Module 3: Regularization and Optimization
points: How deep models are kept from overfitting, and why their training landscapes are difficult: L2 penalties, augmentation, semi-supervised learning, ill-conditioning, local minima, plateaus, saddle points, and flat regions.

slides.title: Module 3 has two big jobs: generalize and train
Regularization controls the gap between training fit and test performance
points: Training error
A high-capacity deep model can fit the training set very closely, sometimes memorizing noise or accidental patterns.
Generalization error
Regularization changes the learning problem so the model is encouraged to perform well on unseen data, not only on the examples it has already seen.
slides.takeaway: A high-capacity deep model can fit the training set very closely, sometimes memorizing noise or accidental patterns.

slides.title: Parameter norm penalties regularize by making large weights costly
points: J̃(θ) = J(θ) + α Ω(θ)
J(θ) is the original training objective.
Ω(θ) is a penalty that measures parameter size.
α controls how strongly the penalty influences learning.
slides.takeaway: Ω(θ) is a penalty that measures parameter size.

slides.title: L2 regularization uses the squared weight norm
points: The penalty grows rapidly as weights become large.
Bias terms are often left unpenalized or treated separately.
The model is encouraged to use smaller, smoother weight values.
slides.takeaway: The penalty grows rapidly as weights become large.

slides.title: L2 regularization appears in updates as weight decay
points: w ← (1 - ηα)w - η ∇w J
η is the learning rate.
α is the L2 regularization strength.
The factor (1 - ηα) shrinks weights before the ordinary gradient step.
slides.takeaway: The factor (1 - ηα) shrinks weights before the ordinary gradient step.

slides.title: L2 regularization biases learning toward simpler mappings
points: Without L2
A network may use large weights to create sharp, highly sensitive input-output behavior.
With L2
Large weights are costly, so the model is nudged toward smoother functions that often generalize better.
slides.takeaway: A network may use large weights to create sharp, highly sensitive input-output behavior.

slides.title: Dataset augmentation increases useful training variation
points: Create additional examples by applying label-preserving transformations.
For images, common transformations include shifts, flips, crops, rotations, color changes, or small noise.
The model sees more variation without requiring manual labeling of every new example.
Augmentation encodes prior knowledge about what should not change the class label.
slides.takeaway: Create additional examples by applying label-preserving transformations.
slides.formula: Create additional examples by applying label-preserving transformations.

slides.title: Augmentation must preserve the meaning of the label
points: Good augmentation
The transformed sample still belongs to the same class and reflects realistic variation expected at test time.
Bad augmentation
The transformation changes the label, creates impossible examples, or teaches invariances the task does not actually have.
slides.takeaway: The transformed sample still belongs to the same class and reflects realistic variation expected at test time.

slides.title: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled data as a training signal
points: Available data
A small labeled dataset is paired with a larger collection of unlabeled examples from the same problem domain.
Learning idea
The model uses unlabeled data to learn structure, representations, or consistency that can improve supervised prediction.
slides.takeaway: A small labeled dataset is paired with a larger collection of unlabeled examples from the same problem domain.

slides.title: Optimization for deep models is hard because the loss surface is complex
points: Deep networks are trained by moving through a high-dimensional parameter space.
The objective can curve sharply in some directions and barely change in others.
Gradients can point in directions that are locally correct but globally inefficient.
The syllabus highlights ill-conditioning, local minima, plateaus, saddle points, and flat regions.
slides.takeaway: Deep networks are trained by moving through a high-dimensional parameter space.
slides.formula: Deep networks are trained by moving through a high-dimensional parameter space.

slides.title: Gradient descent follows local slope, not global understanding
points: θ ← θ - η ∇θ J(θ)
θ represents all trainable parameters.
∇θ J is the gradient of the objective.
η is the learning rate controlling step size.
slides.takeaway: η is the learning rate controlling step size.

slides.title: Ill-conditioning makes some directions much harder than others
points: The problem
The loss surface can have very different curvature along different parameter directions.
Training effect
A step size that is safe in a steep direction may be painfully slow in a flat direction, producing zig-zag or slow progress.
slides.takeaway: The loss surface can have very different curvature along different parameter directions.

slides.title: Ill-conditioning is about curvature, not only about high loss
points: narrow valley
Steep across the valley.
Flat along the valley.
Naive gradient steps can bounce across the steep direction while making slow progress forward.
slides.takeaway: Naive gradient steps can bounce across the steep direction while making slow progress forward.

slides.title: Local minima are points lower than their neighborhood
points: Definition
A local minimum has no nearby direction that immediately decreases the objective, but it may not be the best possible solution overall.
Deep-learning nuance
In high-dimensional deep networks, poor local minima are one concern, but saddle points and flat regions can also be major obstacles.
slides.takeaway: A local minimum has no nearby direction that immediately decreases the objective, but it may not be the best possible solution overall.

slides.title: Plateaus slow learning because gradients become tiny
points: A plateau is a broad region where the objective changes very slowly.
Small gradients produce very small updates.
Training may appear stuck even when it has not reached a good solution.
Momentum, adaptive methods, or better initialization can sometimes help move across plateaus.
slides.takeaway: A plateau is a broad region where the objective changes very slowly.
slides.formula: A plateau is a broad region where the objective changes very slowly.

slides.title: Saddle points can look like minima to first-order methods
points: What a saddle is
A saddle point slopes upward in some directions and downward in others, while the gradient near the point can be very small.
Why it matters
Gradient-based training can slow down near saddle points because the immediate slope gives weak guidance.
slides.takeaway: A saddle point slopes upward in some directions and downward in others, while the gradient near the point can be very small.

slides.title: Flat regions make progress hard to measure
points: Flat regions are areas of parameter space with very low curvature and weak gradients.
Updates can be small even when the model is far from the best parameters.
Flatness can also be connected to many different parameter settings producing similar training loss.
Learning curves may show long stretches of little visible improvement.
slides.takeaway: Flat regions are areas of parameter space with very low curvature and weak gradients.
slides.formula: Updates can be small even when the model is far from the best parameters.

slides.title: Regularization and optimization solve different problems
points: Regularization asks
Will the trained model generalize to unseen examples?
Optimization asks
Can the training procedure find useful parameters efficiently?
slides.takeaway: Will the trained model generalize to unseen examples?

slides.title: Mini activity: diagnose the training problem
points: Show a training curve where training accuracy rises but validation accuracy falls: identify overfitting and suggest regularization.
Show a loss curve with long flat stretches: identify plateau or flat-region behavior.
Show unstable zig-zag loss changes: discuss learning rate and ill-conditioning.
Ask students to name which Module 3 idea applies to each case.
